findings.title: Installer identity check is skipped when Integration does not exist yet
findings.body: GitHubInstallation.dispatch treats Integration.DoesNotExist as success and returns pipeline.next_step() immediately. That is the normal first-install path: the installation webhook often has not created the Integration row before the browser returns with installation_id, and build_integration then creates the Integration and OrganizationIntegration from the caller-supplied installation_id alone. The new comparison of the OAuth login to metadata sender.login only runs after an Integration row already exists and has no OrganizationIntegration. GitHub installation ids are enumerable and webhook delivery is not ordered ahead of the redirect, so an attacker can attach a victim's GitHub App installation to their own Sentry org (or finish the link before the real installer) without ever matching the installer. The control the PR adds fails open on the path it must cover. Finish should be refused until the installer identity is known and matches the OAuth user.

findings.title: Sender comparison crashes when metadata has no sender.login
findings.body: The new check reads integration.metadata["sender"]["login"] with no guard. build_integration only copies sender into metadata when pipeline state already contains it, and this pipeline never binds sender. Integrations created via the API path, or any row written before sender was stored, therefore have no sender dict. On the re-link path (Integration exists, no OrganizationIntegration, status ACTIVE) a missing or non-dict sender raises KeyError or TypeError. That exception is not caught, so the request 500s instead of the installation error page, and a legitimate reinstall of an integration without sender metadata cannot complete. Look up sender.login safely and fail closed with the authenticity error when it is absent.

findings.title: Token exchange omits the redirect_uri sent at authorize time
findings.body: OAuthLoginView adds redirect_uri to the GitHub authorize URL, but the access-token POST only sends code, client_id, and client_secret. GitHub requires the same redirect_uri on the token request when one was supplied during authorization; otherwise the token endpoint returns redirect_uri_mismatch and no access_token. That response is collapsed into the generic authenticity error, so every install fails whenever the authorize redirect_uri is not treated as the app's default callback. Tests stub the token endpoint and never observe this. Send the same redirect_uri on the exchange. The safe_urlopen call and the following get_user_info call are also outside the try that only wraps the body parse, so a connection error or ApiError from GitHub becomes an unhandled 500 instead of that error page.

findings.title: installation_id is written into pipeline state before state is validated
findings.body: OAuthLoginView bind_state's request.GET installation_id before it checks that state equals pipeline.signature, including on requests that have no state at all. PipelineAdvancerView is csrf_protect=False and auth_required=False, and until OAuth finishes the current step is still OAuthLoginView. A cross-site top-level GET to /extensions/github/setup/?installation_id=<attacker> therefore overwrites the victim's in-progress pipeline (SameSite=Lax cookies are sent on that navigation) and then redirects them at GitHub again. The real OAuth callback carries code and state but not installation_id, so GitHubInstallation keeps the poisoned id. A rejected callback has already mutated session state. Bind installation_id only after the OAuth state check succeeds, and do not accept it from an unauthenticated request that is not a completed callback.

findings.title: Installation-not-found test now fails the state check and never hits the 404
findings.body: test_installation_not_found still replaces /app/installations/{id} with a 404, but the follow-up setup request sends state=ddd023d87a913d5226e2a882c4c4cc05. assert_setup_flow in the same file shows a valid pipeline signature is 9cae5e88803f35ed7970fc131e6e65d3. OAuthLoginView rejects any other state before GitHubInstallation or build_integration runs, so the new assertion that the body contains "Invalid installation request." passes because of the state mismatch, not because a missing GitHub installation is handled. The old "The GitHub installation could not be found." assertion was removed, and nothing else drives get_installation_info's 404 path. A break there would not fail CI. Call back with the pipeline's real signature after a successful token exchange and assert the installation-not-found error again.

findings.title: User-mismatch test mutates the webhook body but keeps the old HMAC
findings.body: test_github_user_mismatch changes installation id and sender.login to "attacker" and then posts X-Hub-Signature sha1=d184e6717f8bfbcc291ebc8c0756ee446c6c9486, which cannot be the HMAC of the mutated body. If the webhook view verifies the signature, the post is 401, the assert status_code == 204 fails, and the Integration sender row the test needs is never created. If verification is off in tests, the signature is meaningless. The later assertion only looks for "Invalid installation request.", which is also returned for a bad OAuth state, a bad code, or a missing login. The setup URL reuses state 9cae5e88803f35ed7970fc131e6e65d3 while init_path_2 starts a new pipeline for another organization, so a state failure produces the same page. The test does not show that an OAuth login differing from metadata sender.login is what failed. Recompute the signature for the mutated payload and assert something only the sender comparison path can produce.
